title: Repeating transformations and finite-state patterns
transcript: A finite-state rule has only a limited set of possible situations. Once the same full state occurs again, the same rule repeats everything that follows. Sometimes there is a short starting path before a loop. Count that path separately from the repeating part.

In AMC practice, a repeating transformation might turn a pointer, change a colour or move a mark. Record the complete state between steps. A Mawa style investigation can compare loops from different starting states. Ask which states repeat and which appear only once.
A pointer begins facing north. Turn it clockwise by a quarter turn sixteen times. Where does it point? Count how many quarter turns bring it back to north.
Four turns make one complete revolution. Dividing sixteen by four leaves zero extra turns. Apply those extra turns from north. The pointer ends facing north.
On each press, one dial moves to its next position in a cycle of three. A second dial moves in a cycle of four. After how many presses is the full starting pair first restored?
The first dial resets at multiples of three, and the second at multiples of four. The first positive common reset occurs after twelve presses. The state consists of both dials, not just one.

A machine starts at state one. It moves up through the numbered states until seven. From there its next state is three, and it follows the same rule forever. The starting state is at step zero. Where is it after fifty-eight moves?

At step two the machine first reaches three, the first state of the loop. The earlier states do not recur. The loop has five states. From the loop entry, there are fifty-six more moves to make. Divide by the loop length. The remainder is one. Move that far from the first loop state to reach four.

When counting from the entry time, a remainder of zero means no extra move. That puts the machine at the entry state again. The last state in the loop points back to three, so the calculation never returns to the earlier lead-in states.

A displayed position may not capture the full situation. Include any second dial or change in the rule that affects the next move. The lead-in happens only once. Subtract its length before dividing by the size of the loop.

List the first few complete states and name the next-step rule. Stop when a full state repeats. Separate the first visit to the loop from later laps. Check whether your indexing is by moves from zero or by states from one.
